newsitem.title: CHINA: China may seek off-budget funds to cut deficit.
newsitem.headline: China may seek off-budget funds to cut deficit.

text.p: Government academics have proposed China include off-budget revenue, or revenue that is excluded from the state spending plan, to try to cut the budget deficit, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday.

That change in China's book-keeping system could enable Beijing to meet its target of balancing its budget by the year 2000, a goal that Finance Minister Liu Zhongli said would now be very difficult to achieve.

Some 40 percent of the revenues of central and local governments are not included in the state budget and Beijing must begin to use these funds if it wants to balance the budget, the newspaper quoted Jia Kang, vice-president of the Ministry of Finance Institute of Fiscal Science, as saying.

China's deficit was 60 billion yuan ($7.2 billion) at end-1996, down five billion from the year before and is expected to be cut by four billion in 1997. But that reduction was far slower than targeted, he said.
China's budget deficit accounts for less than one percent of gross domestic product (GDP), a level regarded as very healthy by Western economists.

The proportion of fiscal income in GDP had declined until last year, Jia said. The ratio rose for the first time in 11 years last year, to 10.9 percent, the lowest in the world, he said, but gave no comparative figures.
One major reason for the low ratio was that much of China's income did not show up in the central budget. Jia did not give details of the extra-budget revenues.

However, Liu Rongcang, deputy director of the financial and trade institute under the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, said the imbalance between the central and local governments weakened Beijing's macro-economic control.
Beginning this year, the government will bring 13 major accounts into the budget in a reform that Jia said would increase cash flow.
China had ruled out a tax increase to cut the budget deficit, Jia said. Taxes contribute 90 percent of national revenue, with value-added tax making up 60 percent.

Corporate income tax, reduced recently to 33 percent, could not be raised in the short term, he said. It was also impossible to halt a preferential tax policy of 15 percent for foreign-invested firms in the near future, he said.

State enterprise contributed 70 percent of tax revenue in 1995 while its ratio of GDP fell to 30 percent, said financial expert Xu Yi, adding that it was necessary to expand contributions from the non-state sector, which accounts for less than 30 percent of tax revenue.
Invididual income tax has soared, leaping 88 percent in 1995 and 50 percent in 1996 to 20 billion yuan, but this would have little impact on revenue because of its small base, Jia said.

China could practice fiscal financing and investment -- bringing postal savings, insurance funds and debts guaranteed by the central government into the budget -- to boost revenue, Jia said but gave no further details.
